title: Dry-run: resolution, caching, and a bad TTL
intro: About 4 minutes. Most of DNS is infrastructure you don't write — the one piece of code that matters is what TTL choice actually costs you.

steps.title: Recursive resolution is a chain, not one request
steps.explain: A client's resolver walks root, then TLD, then authoritative server, caching each answer along the way. This is infrastructure the app never implements — but knowing the chain explains why the first lookup after a cache miss is slow and every one after it is fast.

steps.title: The resolver, root, and TLD servers are infra, not app code
steps.explain: Root and TLD servers are operated by registries, not by any application team, and the recursive resolver is usually the OS or ISP's — nothing here is code you deploy. The only lever the app team actually controls is the authoritative server's records and their TTLs.

steps.title: A long TTL is cheap lookups and slow failover
steps.explain: A one-hour TTL means resolvers worldwide cache the answer and barely re-query — great for load, terrible during an incident, because a DNS change to fail over to a new IP takes up to an hour to actually take effect everywhere.
steps.saysOutLoud: TTL is a dial between query load and failover speed, and you have to pick a side deliberately.

steps.title: Fix: lower the TTL before you need fast failover, not during
steps.explain: TTL only helps at failover time if it was already short before the incident started — you can't retroactively shrink a cache that resolvers already populated with the old value. Systems that need fast DNS failover pre-emptively run low TTLs (30-60s) on the records that matter.

steps.title: A stale negative cache can look like an outage
steps.explain: Resolvers cache NXDOMAIN answers too, via the SOA record's negative-cache TTL. Bringing up a brand-new subdomain right after a failed lookup means some resolvers keep returning 'does not exist' until that negative TTL expires, independent of the record's own TTL.

steps.title: GeoDNS routes by resolver location, not by client health
steps.explain: Returning a different answer depending on which regional resolver asked is how DNS-level geo-routing works — it's a static decision made per query, with no visibility into whether the returned region is actually healthy right now, which is why it's usually paired with a health-checked failover layer on top rather than used alone.

closing: If they ask why not just use DNS for all failover: DNS changes propagate on a best-effort basis at the mercy of every resolver's cache along the way — for sub-second failover, put a load balancer or anycast IP in front and let DNS point at that instead of at individual backends.
